home.heading: The universe, one question at a time.
home.subheading: No jargon. No assumptions. Just real astronomy, explored hands-on.

physics_lab.title: Astrophysics Lab
physics_lab.subtitle: Real formulas. Real numbers. Try it before you're told the answer.

escape_velocity.title: Escape Velocity
escape_velocity.prompt: How fast would something need to travel to permanently escape a planet's gravity?
escape_velocity.formula_explainer: This comes from balancing kinetic energy against gravitational potential energy. G is the gravitational constant, M is the planet's mass, and R is its radius from the center.

q1.prompt: If a planet has the same mass as Earth but twice its radius, what happens to its escape velocity?
q1.explain: Escape velocity is inversely proportional to the square root of radius, so a bigger planet of the same mass has a lower escape velocity — gravity is spread over a larger surface.

q2.prompt: What does the escape velocity formula NOT depend on?
q2.explain: v = √(2GM/R) depends only on mass and radius — not on launch direction, since it's a scalar minimum speed.

q3.prompt: Why is Jupiter's escape velocity so much higher than Earth's?
q3.opt2: Jupiter is closer to the Sun
q3.explain: Jupiter's huge mass (about 318 Earths) dominates the formula, giving it a far higher escape velocity (~59.5 km/s) despite also having a much larger radius.

q4.prompt: If you could double a planet's mass while keeping its radius the same, what happens to escape velocity?
q4.explain: Since v ∝ √M, doubling mass multiplies escape velocity by √2 (about 1.41×), not by 2.

q5.prompt: Does escape velocity depend on the mass of the object trying to escape (like a rocket)?
q5.opt1: Yes, heavier rockets need higher escape velocity
q5.opt2: No, it's the same for any object regardless of its own mass
q5.opt3: Only for objects heavier than 1000 kg
q5.explain: Escape velocity comes from energy balance where the escaping object's mass cancels out of the equation — it's the same for a pebble or a spacecraft.

q6.prompt: The Moon's escape velocity is about 2.4 km/s, much lower than Earth's 11.2 km/s. Why?
q6.opt1: The Moon has far less mass and a smaller radius than Earth
q6.opt3: The Moon is farther from the Sun
q6.explain: The Moon's much smaller mass (about 1.2% of Earth's) reduces GM far more than its smaller radius increases escape velocity, giving a much lower net value.

orbital_velocity.title: Orbital Velocity
orbital_velocity.prompt: How fast does something need to move sideways to stay in a stable circular orbit, without falling in or flying away?
orbital_velocity.formula_explainer: This balances the centripetal force needed for circular motion against gravity's pull. It depends on mass and radius similarly to escape velocity — in fact orbital velocity always equals escape velocity divided by √2.
orbital_velocity.sanity_check: Real value for the ISS (~400 km altitude): ≈ 7.7 km/s

q1.prompt: How does orbital velocity compare to escape velocity at the same distance?
q1.opt2: It's the same as escape velocity
q1.explain: Escape velocity is exactly √2 times orbital velocity at any given radius — this falls directly out of comparing the two formulas.

q2.prompt: The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km altitude. Why doesn't it fall to Earth?
q2.opt1: It's moving sideways fast enough that its fall matches Earth's curvature
q2.opt2: There's no gravity at that altitude
q2.opt3: Its engines constantly push it upward
q2.explain: Orbit is really continuous falling — the ISS moves sideways at ~7.7 km/s, fast enough that as it falls, the ground curves away at the same rate.

q3.prompt: If a satellite orbits closer to Earth, what happens to its required orbital velocity?
q3.explain: Since v = √(GM/r), a smaller orbital radius r means a larger orbital velocity is needed to maintain the orbit.

q4.prompt: Geostationary satellites orbit much higher (~35,786 km) than the ISS. Is their orbital velocity higher or lower?
q4.explain: At a much larger radius, orbital velocity is lower — geostationary satellites move at about 3.1 km/s, versus the ISS's 7.7 km/s.

q5.prompt: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in orbit?
q5.opt1: Gravity from the body it orbits
q5.explain: Gravity itself supplies exactly the centripetal force needed for circular motion at the correct orbital velocity — no continuous thrust is required.

q6.prompt: Orbital velocity around the Sun at Earth's distance is about 29.8 km/s. What does this represent?
q6.opt1: How fast Earth spins on its axis
q6.opt2: How fast Earth travels around the Sun
q6.explain: 29.8 km/s is Earth's orbital velocity around the Sun — the speed needed to maintain a stable orbit at 1 AU.

kepler.title: Kepler's Third Law
kepler.prompt: How does a planet's distance from the Sun relate to how long its year is?
kepler.formula_explainer: Discovered by Johannes Kepler in 1619: the square of a planet's orbital period equals the cube of its distance, when period is in years and distance is in AU around the Sun.
kepler.sanity_check: Real value for Mars (1.52 AU): ≈ 1.88 years

q1.prompt: A planet orbits the Sun at 4 AU. Roughly how long is its year?
q1.explain: T² = a³, so T² = 4³ = 64, and T = √64 = 8 years.

q2.prompt: Which planet has a longer year: one closer to the Sun, or one farther away?
q2.explain: T² ∝ a³ means greater distance always means a longer orbital period — farther planets take longer to complete one orbit.

q3.prompt: Mercury orbits at about 0.39 AU. Roughly how long is its year?
q3.explain: T² = 0.39³ ≈ 0.059, so T ≈ √0.059 ≈ 0.24 years — matching Mercury's real 88-day year closely.

q4.prompt: Kepler's Third Law in this simple form (T² = a³) works exactly for which case?
q4.opt1: Only objects orbiting the Sun, with T in years and a in AU
q4.opt2: Any two orbiting objects anywhere in the universe
q4.explain: This simplified form only holds for objects orbiting the Sun with those specific units — a more general version includes both masses for other systems.

q5.prompt: Why was Kepler's Third Law historically important?
q5.opt1: It gave the first mathematical relationship connecting orbital distances and times, later explained by Newton's gravity
q5.opt2: It proved the Sun was the center of the universe with no exceptions
q5.opt3: It disproved the existence of comets
q5.explain: Kepler's laws described planetary motion precisely from observation, and later became a cornerstone that Newton's theory of gravity successfully explained from first principles.

q6.prompt: A hypothetical planet takes 27 years to orbit the Sun. Roughly how far out is it (in AU)?

inverse_square.title: Inverse-Square Law of Light
inverse_square.prompt: How much dimmer does a star look if you're twice as far away from it?
inverse_square.formula_explainer: A star's brightness falls off with the square of distance — double the distance, and you get only a quarter of the light, because the same light spreads over 4 times the area.
inverse_square.sanity_check: At 2× the distance, brightness drops to 25% of the original.

q1.prompt: If you triple your distance from a star, how much dimmer does it appear?
q1.explain: Brightness falls with the square of distance, so 3× the distance means 3² = 9 times dimmer.

q2.prompt: Two identical stars are the same actual brightness, but Star A looks dimmer than Star B from Earth. What does this most likely tell you?
q2.explain: For stars of identical true brightness (luminosity), the inverse-square law means the dimmer-looking one is simply farther away — this is actually how astronomers estimate distances using 'standard candles'.

q3.prompt: If you move to 4 times the distance from a light source, how much of the original brightness remains?
q3.explain: Brightness falls with the square of distance: at 4× distance, brightness is 1/4² = 1/16 of the original.

q4.prompt: Why does the inverse-square law involve an area (4πd²) in its formula?
q4.opt1: Light spreads out over an ever-larger sphere as it travels, and that sphere's surface area grows with distance squared
q4.opt3: It's just a mathematical convenience with no physical meaning
q4.explain: Light radiates outward in all directions, spreading over the surface of an expanding sphere. Since a sphere's surface area is 4πd², the same total light gets diluted over an area that grows with d².

q5.prompt: This same inverse-square pattern also applies to which other force?
q5.explain: Gravity also follows an inverse-square law (F ∝ 1/r²) — it's one of several fundamental phenomena in physics that spread outward the same geometric way.

q6.prompt: Astronomers use the inverse-square law with 'standard candles' (stars of known true brightness) mainly to measure what?
q6.explain: By comparing a standard candle's known true brightness to how dim it appears, astronomers can calculate distance directly from the inverse-square relationship.

wien.title: Wien's Law
wien.prompt: What color does an object glow, based purely on its temperature?
wien.formula_explainer: Wien's Law says the wavelength at which an object radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its temperature. Hotter objects peak at shorter (bluer) wavelengths; cooler objects peak at longer (redder) ones.
wien.sanity_check: The Sun (~5,778 K) peaks at about 501 nm — in the visible blue-green part of the spectrum.

q1.prompt: As an object gets hotter, what happens to its peak wavelength?
q1.explain: Wien's Law is an inverse relationship — higher temperature means shorter peak wavelength, which is why very hot stars look blue-white.

q2.prompt: A star with a surface temperature of about 3,000 K would appear mostly what color?
q2.explain: Cooler stars (like red dwarfs, around 2,500–3,700 K) peak at longer, redder wavelengths according to Wien's Law.

q3.prompt: A star with a surface temperature of about 20,000 K would appear mostly what color?
q3.explain: Hot stars (B-type, 10,000–30,000 K) peak at short wavelengths, appearing blue-white — the opposite end of the spectrum from cool red stars.

q4.prompt: Wien's Law uses the constant b ≈ 2,897,771 nm·K. What role does this constant play?
q4.opt1: It converts temperature directly into peak wavelength via division
q4.opt2: It has no real physical meaning, just a scaling number
q4.opt3: It only applies to the Sun specifically
q4.explain: Wien's displacement constant (b) is a universal physical constant — dividing it by any temperature in Kelvin gives that object's peak emission wavelength.

q5.prompt: Does Wien's Law apply only to stars?
q5.opt1: No — it applies to any object that radiates as a blackbody, including planets and even human bodies
q5.opt2: Yes, it only works for stars
q5.opt3: It only works for objects hotter than the Sun
q5.explain: Wien's Law is a general blackbody radiation law. It's why thermal cameras can detect the infrared glow of comparatively cool objects like human bodies, which peak in infrared, not visible light.

q6.prompt: If a star's peak wavelength shifts to be shorter over time, what has likely happened to its temperature?
q6.opt3: Temperature and peak wavelength are unrelated
q6.explain: Wien's Law is an inverse relationship — a shift to shorter (bluer) peak wavelength means the object has gotten hotter.

stefan_boltzmann.title: Stefan–Boltzmann Law
stefan_boltzmann.prompt: How bright is a star, really, based on its size and temperature?
stefan_boltzmann.formula_explainer: A star's total light output (luminosity) depends on both its surface area and temperature. Since L ∝ R²T⁴, temperature matters enormously — doubling temperature increases luminosity 16-fold.
stefan_boltzmann.sanity_check: At Sun-like radius and temperature (1× each), luminosity should read almost exactly 1.

q1.prompt: If you double a star's temperature while keeping its radius the same, how much brighter does it get?
q1.explain: Luminosity depends on T⁴, so doubling temperature increases luminosity by 2⁴ = 16 times.

q2.prompt: If you double a star's radius while keeping its temperature the same, how much brighter does it get?
q2.explain: Luminosity depends on R², so doubling radius increases luminosity by 2² = 4 times.

q3.prompt: A red giant is cooler than the Sun but far more luminous. How is this possible?
q3.opt1: Its enormous radius more than makes up for its lower temperature
q3.opt2: It's actually hotter than it looks
q3.opt3: Red giants don't follow the Stefan-Boltzmann law
q3.explain: Since luminosity depends on R², a huge radius can outweigh a lower T⁴ term — this is exactly why red giants, despite cooler surfaces, shine far brighter than the Sun.

q4.prompt: Why does temperature (T⁴) affect luminosity so much more strongly than radius (R²)?
q4.opt1: Because it's raised to the 4th power instead of the 2nd, so small temperature changes compound faster
q4.opt2: Temperature doesn't really affect luminosity much at all
q4.opt3: This is only true for stars, not other objects
q4.explain: A 4th-power relationship grows far faster than a squared one — this is a general feature of blackbody radiation, not unique to stars.

q5.prompt: Two stars have the same luminosity. One is much hotter. What must be true of the hotter one?
q5.opt1: It must have a smaller radius
q5.opt2: It must have a larger radius
q5.explain: Since L ∝ R²T⁴, if luminosity is equal but T is higher, R must be smaller to balance the equation — this is exactly how white dwarfs (hot, tiny) can match the luminosity of larger, cooler stars.

universe_explorer.title: Universe Explorer
universe_explorer.subtitle: The universe is mostly empty space — filled with a few kinds of extraordinary things.
universe_explorer.scale_instruction: Drag the slider to zoom out — from a planet to the edge of what we can observe.

galaxies.name: Galaxies
galaxies.description: A galaxy is a vast, gravity-bound collection of billions of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter. Our own galaxy, the Milky Way, is a barred spiral holding an estimated 100–400 billion stars — and it's just one of roughly two trillion galaxies in the observable universe.

nebulae.name: Nebulae
nebulae.description: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space. Some, like the Orion Nebula, are stellar nurseries where gravity slowly pulls material together to form new stars. Others are the glowing remains left behind after a star dies.

black_holes.name: Black Holes
black_holes.description: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the event horizon. They form when massive stars collapse. Supermassive versions, millions of times the Sun's mass, sit at the centers of most galaxies, including our own (Sagittarius A*).

stars.name: Stars
stars.description: A star is a massive ball of plasma held together by its own gravity, generating light and heat by fusing hydrogen into helium at its core. Our Sun is a fairly average star — one of hundreds of billions in the Milky Way alone.

supernovae.name: Supernovae
supernovae.description: A supernova is the explosive death of a massive star, briefly outshining its entire host galaxy. These explosions forge and scatter heavy elements — like the iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones — throughout the universe.

star_clusters.name: Star Clusters
star_clusters.description: Stars often form and travel in groups. Open clusters, like the Pleiades, are young and loosely bound, with a few hundred stars. Globular clusters are far older and denser, tightly packing tens of thousands to millions of stars into a compact sphere.

cmb.name: Cosmic Microwave Background
cmb.description: Faint radiation left over from about 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe first became transparent to light. Discovered by accident in 1965, it fills all of space at a nearly uniform temperature of about 2.7 K.

dark_matter.name: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
dark_matter.description: Roughly 95% of the universe isn't made of the atoms we know. Dark matter, inferred from its gravitational pull on galaxies, makes up about 27%. Dark energy, which drives the universe's accelerating expansion, makes up roughly 68%. Both remain among astronomy's biggest open questions.

solar_system.name: The Solar System
solar_system.description: Our home system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. It holds the Sun, 8 planets, over 200 moons, the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, and the icy Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune.

comets.name: Comets
comets.description: Comets are icy leftovers from the outer solar system's formation. As they near the Sun, ice on their surface vaporizes, creating a glowing coma and a tail that always points away from the Sun. Halley's Comet, the most famous, returns roughly every 76 years.

habitable_zone.name: The Habitable Zone
habitable_zone.description: Often called the 'Goldilocks zone,' this is the range of distances from a star where a planet could be warm enough for liquid water but not so hot that it boils away. Earth sits comfortably inside the Sun's habitable zone.

andromeda.name: The Andromeda Galaxy
andromeda.description: The nearest large galaxy to our own, about 2.5 million light-years away, and visible to the naked eye as a faint smudge on a dark night. It's a spiral galaxy like the Milky Way, and the two are on a slow collision course, expected to merge in roughly 4.5 billion years.

earth.label: Earth
earth.blurb: Your home planet — and the baseline for everything that follows.

sun.label: The Sun
sun.blurb: About 109 Earths could line up across the Sun's diameter.

solar_system.label: The Solar System
solar_system.blurb: 1 AU (Astronomical Unit) is the Earth–Sun distance: about 150 million km.

nearest_star.label: To the nearest star system
nearest_star.blurb: Even at the speed of light, it would take over 4 years to reach Alpha Centauri.

milky_way.label: The Milky Way
milky_way.blurb: Our entire galaxy — and we're just one star among hundreds of billions in it.

observable_universe.label: The Observable Universe
observable_universe.blurb: The furthest we can possibly see, limited by the age of the universe and the speed of light.

q1.prompt: Which of these forges the heavy elements found throughout the universe, including in living things?
q1.explain: Supernova explosions create and scatter heavy elements across space — many atoms in your own body were forged this way.

q2.prompt: What does the Cosmic Microwave Background tell us about?
q2.opt1: The current temperature of the Sun
q2.opt2: The universe when it was about 380,000 years old
q2.opt3: The location of the nearest black hole
q2.explain: The CMB is leftover radiation from a specific early moment in the universe's history, giving us a direct snapshot of conditions back then.

sky_explorer.title: Sky Explorer
sky_explorer.subtitle: What's actually happening above you tonight.

moon.heading: Tonight's Moon
moon.explainer: The Moon doesn't produce its own light — we see it because it reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth roughly every 29.5 days, the portion we see lit up changes, giving us the cycle of phases.

planets.heading: Planets you can actually see
planets.text: Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn are often bright enough to see without any telescope. A simple way to tell a planet from a star: planets usually shine with a steady light, while stars twinkle — because starlight travels much further and gets disturbed more by our atmosphere.

constellations.heading: A few constellations to start with

ursa_major.name: Ursa Major (the Great Bear)
ursa_major.text: Contains the "Big Dipper," one of the most recognizable star patterns in the northern sky. Its two end stars point almost directly at Polaris, the North Star.

orion.name: Orion (the Hunter)
orion.text: Easiest to spot by its three-star belt in a straight line. Visible from most of the world, making it one of the best constellations for beginners.

cassiopeia.name: Cassiopeia
cassiopeia.text: Forms a clear "W" or "M" shape depending on the season, and sits roughly opposite the Big Dipper across Polaris.

q1.prompt: Why does the Moon go through phases?
q1.opt1: Because we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth
q1.opt2: Because Earth's shadow covers it every night
q1.explain: The Moon's phases come from our changing view of the half that's lit by the Sun — the Moon itself doesn't change shape.

q2.prompt: What's a simple way to tell a planet from a star in the night sky?
q2.opt3: Stars are only visible in winter
q2.explain: Starlight twinkles because it travels much farther and gets disturbed more by our atmosphere; planets usually shine with a steadier light.

exoplanet_hunter.title: Exoplanet Hunter
exoplanet_hunter.subtitle: Find a planet by watching starlight dim — this is the transit method, and it's how most known exoplanets were discovered.
exoplanet_hunter.instruction: One of these three light curves shows a planet passing in front of its star. Which one?
exoplanet_hunter.correct: Correct — that dip is a transit.
exoplanet_hunter.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a brief, symmetric dip in brightness, then look again.
exoplanet_hunter.explanation: When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view, it blocks a tiny fraction of the star's light, causing a small, temporary, repeating dip in brightness. This is the transit method — it's how missions like Kepler and TESS have found thousands of exoplanets.

size_challenge.heading: Now estimate the planet's size
size_challenge.instruction: The depth of the dip relates directly to the planet's size compared to its star: depth = (planet radius / star radius)². Adjust the dip depth below and see the size ratio update.

q1.prompt: If a light curve shows a deeper dip, what does that suggest about the planet?
q1.opt2: It's larger relative to its star
q1.explain: Since dip depth = (planet radius / star radius)², a deeper dip directly means a proportionally larger planet relative to its star.

asteroid_hunter.title: Asteroid Hunter
asteroid_hunter.subtitle: Spot the object that moved — this is how astronomers really find asteroids.
asteroid_hunter.instruction: These two star fields were captured a short time apart. Stars stay fixed — but one object moved. Click it in Frame 2.
asteroid_hunter.frame2_label: Frame 2 — click the object that moved
asteroid_hunter.correct: Found it. That's how a moving object gives itself away against a fixed background of stars.
asteroid_hunter.incorrect: Not that one — look for the dot that's in a different position between the two frames.
asteroid_hunter.explanation: Real astronomers use this exact technique, called "blink comparison": they compare images of the same patch of sky taken minutes or hours apart. Stars are so far away they appear fixed, but a nearby asteroid visibly shifts position — that's the giveaway.
asteroid_hunter.simulated_label: Simulated for learning purposes — not a real sky image

q1.prompt: Why does an asteroid appear to move between two images of the same sky patch, while stars don't?
q1.opt1: Asteroids are much closer to Earth than stars are
q1.opt3: Stars are too small to photograph
q1.explain: Because asteroids are relatively close, their position against the fixed background of much more distant stars visibly shifts over time — this is the basis of the blink comparison method.

stellar_detective.title: Stellar Detective
stellar_detective.subtitle: A star's color is a direct readout of its surface temperature.
stellar_detective.question: Based on this temperature, what spectral class is this star?
stellar_detective.incorrect: Not quite — check the temperature ranges below and try again.
stellar_detective.explainer: Astronomers classify stars into spectral types — O, B, A, F, G, K, M, from hottest to coolest — based on temperature, which also determines color. Hotter stars glow blue-white; cooler stars glow orange-red. Our Sun is a G-type star, at around 5,778 K.

q1.prompt: Which spectral class is our Sun?
q1.explain: The Sun is a G-type star, with a surface temperature of about 5,778 K — putting it right in the yellow part of the spectrum.
